title: The social versus food preference test: A behavioral paradigm for studying competing motivated behaviors in rodents
author: Reppucci, Veenema

steps.title: Construct and prepare apparatus
steps.instruction: Build or obtain a three‑chamber arena sized for rats (40 cm × 40 cm × 27 cm) or mice (30 cm × 30 cm × 20 cm) with a translucent acrylic partition opening (rats 10 cm × 10.2 cm; mice 5 cm × 5 cm). Walls should be opaque (paint or Con‑Tact paper) to reduce visual distractions; ensure the exterior color contrasts with the animal colour if using tracking software. Use custom corrals: rats – rectangular 18 cm W × 10 cm D × 21 cm H with 0.6 cm bars spaced 1.75 cm; mice – cylindrical 8.5 cm ID × 10.5 cm OD × 17 cm H with 0.6 cm bars spaced 1.5 cm. Corrals allow olfactory, visual and auditory contact but limit tactile contact.

steps.title: Clean apparatus and corrals
steps.instruction: At the start and end of each day, wipe the arena with 70 % ethanol and wipe corrals with a dilute cleaning solution. Repeat cleaning between each subject.

steps.title: Habituate experimental subjects
steps.instruction: 1–2 days before testing, place each subject in the centre chamber of the empty arena with empty corrals at opposite ends. Allow free exploration for 10 min while video‑recording. Measure time spent in each chamber; cohort averages should show no side bias.

steps.title: Habituate stimulus animals
steps.instruction: In separate trials, confine each stimulus animal in its corral for 10 min, then return to its home cage.

steps.title: Pre‑test preparation on test day
steps.instruction: Remove food from the cages of stimulus animals 2 h before testing. If the test room differs from the housing room, move subjects to the test room at least 1 h before the test to acclimatize. Clean the arena and corrals again. Set up a camera (e.g., Logitech HD Pro‑C910) on the ceiling, connected to a computer in an adjoining room. Position the camera directly overhead; ensure even illumination and minimal glare. Use overhead white light for light‑phase testing or infrared/indirect dim red light for dark‑phase testing. Verify that the arena colour contrasts with the animal colour for automated tracking.

steps.title: Place stimuli in corrals
steps.instruction: Insert the selected social stimulus (unfamiliar, age/sex/species‑matched conspecific) into one corral and the food stimulus (standard laboratory chow, Teklad Irradiated 22/5 Rodent Diet, 8940; ~8 pellets for mice, ~20 pellets for rats) into the other. Position corrals on opposite ends of the arena (e.g., middle of back wall or back corner). Counterbalance left/right placement across subjects and, when applicable, across test days within subjects. Move food away from the corral edges to prevent consumption.

steps.title: Run the social‑versus‑food test
steps.instruction: Start video recording, then place the experimental subject into the centre chamber. Allow free exploration for 10 min. Monitor from outside the test room; if the animal climbs onto a corral or the arena edge, give ~10 s to climb down. If it does not descend, gently pick it up and place it on the floor of the chamber it climbed out of (not the centre chamber).

steps.title: End test and clean
steps.instruction: Stop recording after 10 min. Return the subject to its home cage. Remove the social stimulus and return it to its home cage; discard the food stimulus. Clean the arena and corrals as described, then reset (starting at “Place stimuli in corrals”) for the next subject.

steps.title: Automated behavioral scoring
steps.instruction: Use tracking software (e.g., AnyMaze, Stoelting) to quantify: (a) time spent in each of the three chambers; (b) time spent in the investigation zone around each corral (rats: head within 6 cm of corral edge; mice: centre‑mass within 5 cm of corral edge). Troubleshoot glare, camera angle, animal‑stimulus contrast, or climbing if tracking fails.

steps.title: Manual behavioral scoring
steps.instruction: If needed, score videos with Solomon Coder (https://solomon.andraspeter.com/). Record: (a) time in each chamber; (b) active investigation time—defined as head/gaze directed toward the stimulus with nose‑poking, pawing, or sniffing. For food, count only investigation of the bottom of the corral; for social stimulus, include rearing if attention is clearly on the conspecific. Score blind to subject sex, treatment, and stimulus identity when possible. Compute preference scores as ((social time)/(social + food time))*100; values > 50 % indicate a social preference, < 50 % a food preference.

description: The Social versus Food Preference Test was validated by examining how acute food deprivation would alter stimulus preference, under the assumption that food deprivation would increase motivation for food and thus bias preference more towards the food stimulus [1,6,7]. Experimental subjects were individually housed adult (13–14 week old) Wistar rats (n = 7 males, n = 5 females) and C57BL/6 mice (n = 8 males, n = 6 females) [2]. All housing and testing was in accordance with the National Institute of Health Guidelines for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the Michigan State University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Experimental subjects were first habituated to the testing apparatus as described above, and then tested in the Social versus Food Preference Test on two occasions each 48 hrs apart using a within-subjects counterbalanced design (sated × food-deprived). The length of food deprivation was 24 hrs for rats and 18 hrs for mice (per IACUC recommendation and pilot testing to ensure subjects would not lose more than 15% of their body weight). The social stimulus was an unfamiliar age-, sex-, and species-matched conspecific, and each social stimulus was used twice per day in non-successive tests to reduce the number of animals used. The food stimulus was standard laboratory chow (Teklad Irradiated 22/5 Rodent Diet, 8940; ~8 pellets for mice, ~20 pellets for rats). A webcam (Logitech HD Pro-C910) was attached to the ceiling and connected to a PC computer in an adjoining room to record the habituation and test sessions. All other methods were as described above. Automated behavioral tracking software (AnyMaze, Stoelting) was used to quantify the amount of time experimental subjects spent in each of the three chambers, and the amount of time experimental subjects spent in designated investigation zones around the corrals (rats: head placement within 6 cm of corral edge, mice: center mass placement within 5 cm of corral edge; Fig. 1A).
